name: Ngawun
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.

new_statements.quote: The main stress on a word is almost always on the first syllable. Occasionally there is a secondary stress on the second syllable of a trisyllabic word. In a four-syllable word there may be a secondary stress on the third syllable, especially if the word is a reduplicated form. In a longer word secondary stress tends to fall on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme, if any (for example [ˈkalamùndu] 'grass-ABL'), or otherwise on odd-numbered non-final syllables (e.g. [wánatYùŋkari] 'moon'). For purposes of stress the first vowel of suffixes of the form -VC(C)V normally counts as part of the preceding morpheme. [...] The word /puriŋkir/ 'tomorrow' is exceptional in that the main stress frequently falls on the second syllable, the first vowel then being centralised to [ə] and often reduced

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word (almost without exception). Secondary stress: in trisyllables occasionally on the second syllable; in four-syllable words possibly on the third (especially reduplications); in longer words on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme if there is one, otherwise on odd-numbered non-final syllables. For stress-counting, the first vowel of a -VC(C)V suffix belongs to the preceding morpheme (thus [ímbamìriŋgi], not [ímbamɪrìŋgi]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, described in detail: 3-syllable words occasionally sigma2; 4-syllable words may have sigma3 (esp. reduplicated forms); longer words: first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme if any, else odd-numbered non-final syllables (wánatYùŋkari 'moon' = 10100). Suffix-initial vowels of -VC(C)V suffixes count with the preceding morpheme for stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: /puriŋkir/ 'tomorrow' frequently takes main stress on the second syllable with the initial vowel reduced to [ə] ([pəríŋkər]); Breen notes this is a common Australian pattern for words of 3+ syllables beginning with a peripheral stop/nasal followed by V + lateral/rhotic (cf. old spellings 'bringar', 'blagura' for /pulakara/ 'two'). Nothing can be said about sentence stress or intonation because of the single speaker's hesitant speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen's Ngawun phonology (Chapter 2) is based on a lexicon of 'a little over 300 words' from a single speaker, Miss Cherry O'Keefe; the stress section (2.3) is explicitly about Ngawun, not the other Mayi communalects (Mayi-Kulan, Mayi-Yapi, Mayi-Thakurti, Wunumara, Mayi-Kutuna), for which §2.5 (p. 29) says little can be said about phonological differences from Ngawun and makes no stress statement. The book covers all Mayi communalects; the open excerpt's Rosetta metadata tags it ISO nxn = Ngawun.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (dominant set only: initial primary, default odd-count secondary stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 (1 = a stressed syllable) window 2-5, outside the strict set as morphology-conditioned) rests on Breen 1981:25, the only and best available description of this extinct language, held at page-image grade and re-verified now (p.5 = printed p.25; quotation verbatim). The page supports the classification as the deep note framed it: primary stress 'almost always' initial; secondary hedged ('occasionally', 'may', 'tends') and morphology-first in longer words (bound-morpheme clause outranks odd-count clause; ikalamundu 10010 vs wanatjungkari 10100 at 5 syllables), one exceptional word purinkir with second-syllable main stress. Nothing found suggests a better source exists. The weakness is record hygiene, not sourcing: the catalog row carries empty quote/cite/loc/grade fields and no 'sources' entry even though the note and held scan supp

tone.quote: 2.3 Stress and intonation. The main stress on a word is almost always on the first syllable. Occasionally there is a secondary stress on the second syllable of a trisyllabic word. [...] The word /puṛiŋkir/ 'tomorrow' is exceptional in that the main stress frequently falls on the second syllable, the first vowel then being centralised to [ə] and often reduced, thus [pəṛíŋkər]. [...] Because of the hesitancy of Miss O'Keefe's speech there seems to be nothing worthwhile that can be said about sentence stress or intonation.
